To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
national electronic health record systems can be viewed as `wicked projects' that are difficult to define, have no clear solution and can be characterized by high levels of conflict.
the Australian government's National e-Health Strategy, as it was conceived in 2008, was not a `wicked project'.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the management of `wicked' projects and suggests a new way of thinking about them.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Australian experience with the National Electronic Health Records System is that it is not a `wicked project' in itself, but it has been made so by the political and bureaucratic environment in which it has been created.

the National eHealth Record System (NeHRS) is a complex, wicked project that has been subject to a series of failed attempts at implementation, and that it will require significant changes in the way that it is managed in order to succeed.
national electronic health record systems are `wicked projects' and should be approached with care and understanding.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

there are a number of key lessons to be learnt for future projects of this type, including the importance of: •	recognizing the `wickedness' of the problem; •	involving all stakeholders; •	using a systems approach to design and implementation; •	developing an effective governance model; •	ensuring a clear business case; •	develop a comprehensive change management plan; •	recognize the importance of data quality; •	recognise the importance of privacy and security
the National eHealth record system has been a failure.
the National Electronic Health Record System (NEHRS) is not a `wicked project'.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the `wicked' nature of the problem should be recognized from the outset, and that the project management should be adapted to cope with this nature.
the `wickedness' of these projects should be acknowledged and managed, and the project team should be given the flexibility to adapt to the changing needs of the project as it progresses.
the complexity and `messiness' inherent in large scale ICT projects needs to be recognized, managed and dealt with, and not simply swept under the carpet.
